query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a CrCoNiFe-based high-entropy alloy produced by directed energy deposition (DED), substituting ~5% of the alloying elements with Mo will concurrently improve mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline CrCoNiFe HEA (Cantor-type) manufactured via DED with no Mo addition.
generation.intervention: Addition of approximately 5 wt% Mo (replacing a portion of Cr or equivalent) during powder blending for DED processing.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature ambient conditions and exposure to a 3.5 wt% NaCl saline solution; mechanical testing performed at slow strain rates suitable for room-temperature creep evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mo-induced σ-phase particles and preferential segregation at grain boundaries, leading to refined microstructure and improved passivation film formation.
generation.mechanism: Mo addition promotes grain-boundary pinning and microstructural refinement that reduces dislocation mobility (improving creep resistance) while stabilizing protective oxide films to enhance corrosion resistance; the combined effect also boosts yield strength and durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Approximately 20% increase in yield strength and a measurable decrease in room-temperature creep rate, with corrosion rates reduced by roughly 30% relative to the untreated HEA.
generation.baseline: CrCoNiFe HEA produced by DED without Mo addition.
generation.boundary: Benefits are expected up to about 10% Mo; beyond that, excessive Mo could induce brittleness or unwanted precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum Mo concentration and potential trade-offs with ductility remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of DED-produced CrCoNiFe HEA samples – one without Mo and one with 5% Mo addition. Subject both sets to standardized tensile tests, room-temperature creep tests (under a constant load at ambient temperature), and potentiodynamic polarization tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Room-temperature creep strain rate and time-to-failure under constant load
Corrosion current density and corrosion potential via polarization curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 5% Mo-doped samples do not show at least a 15% improvement in yield strength and a significant reduction in both creep strain rate and corrosion current density (i.e., improvements less than 15–20% over baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. CrMnFeCoNi, a type of Cantor alloy, is known for its exceptional strength in cryogenic environments, rendering it an optimal choice for low-temperature applications []. HEAs with high chromium (Cr) and molybdenum (Mo) content are gaining popularity in marine engineering due to their exceptional corrosion resistance, which is critical. HEAs exhibit outstanding structural stability and mechanical properties as a result of their slow diffusion rate and lattice strain effect. The lattice strain effect, which is induced by atomic size mismatches when combining various elements, enhances the strength and resistance to deformation []. The microstructure remains stable at elevated temperatures due to the slow diffusion rate, which improves both corrosion resistance and low-temperature strength. Additive manufacturing (AM) is a process that involves the layer-by-layer deposition of wire or metal powder using a high-energy heat source, such as a laser or electron beam []. AM techniques can be classified into two main groups: directed energy deposition (DED) and powder bed fusion (PBF). PBF employs a laser to target specific regions of metal powder on a substrate []. The high temperature tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy, i.e., high entropy superalloy (HESA) have been investigated. Comparing to those of the reported high entropy alloys, HESA possesses outstanding tensile yield strength from ambient to elevated temperatures. Furthermore, the creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C can be compared to those of Ni-based superalloys such as RENE′ 80 and NX-188 DS, so the potential of HESA for high temperature applications is demonstrated in this article. papers.title: New HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by Electrospark Deposition with High Corrosion Resistance.
papers.system: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy used as a coating on stainless steel
papers.approach: Electrospark deposition (ESD) of mechanically alloyed, spark plasma sintered HEA powders under an argon atmosphere
papers.findings: The coating demonstrated high corrosion resistance in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution along with improved hardness compared to the substrate; rapid cooling during ESD minimized oxidation and contamination.
papers.mechanism: The argon atmosphere and rapid cooling during deposition yield a homogeneous, low-oxygen, high-purity coating that enhances corrosion resistance and surface mechanical durability.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Post heat treatment with a reduced cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundaries
papers.findings: At 650°C testing, serrated grain boundaries increased tensile fracture strain by a factor of 3.5 and crept rupture life by a factor of 400 compared to a straight grain boundary system.
papers.mechanism: Coarsening of γ′ precipitates during slow cooling causes interference with mobile grain boundaries, leading to a serrated morphology that distributes strain more evenly and hinders intergranular crack propagation.

papers.title: Effects of Mo Addition on Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of Cr<sub>25-x</sub>Co<sub>25</sub>Ni<sub>25</sub>Fe<sub>25</sub>Mo<sub>x</sub> High…
papers.system: CrCoNiFe-based high-entropy alloy (Cantor-type) modified with Mo (with x = 0, 5, 10%) manufactured by directed energy deposition (DED)
papers.approach: Elemental substitution via controlled Mo addition (increasing Mo content from 0 to 10%) during powder-based DED processing
papers.findings: Addition of 5% Mo increased yield strength by ~20% and ultimate tensile strength by ~9.5% versus the Mo-free baseline; 10% Mo yielded even higher strength improvements, while potentiodynamic tests in 3.5% NaCl solution showed improved corrosion performance, likely owing to modified passivation behavior.
papers.mechanism: Mo segregates to grain boundaries and promotes the formation and stabilization of σ-phase particles that refine grains and enhance passivation film formation, thereby improving both mechanical strength and corrosion resistance.

papers.title: The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with FCC matrix and L12 precipitates
papers.approach: Designing a microstructure analogous to Ni-based superalloys with a high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates; discussion includes potential for minor additions (e.g., Mo) to tailor lattice misfit and rafting behavior
papers.findings: HESA exhibits outstanding tensile yield strength across room to elevated temperatures and demonstrates competitive creep rupture lives (e.g., ≈114 hours at 982°C) compared to conventional superalloys.
papers.mechanism: Strength is attributed to a combination of low stacking fault energy, high anti-phase boundary energy, and stable γ′ precipitates; discussions suggest that minor Mo additions could further regulate lattice misfit for improved creep behavior.

papers.title: A strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy resists hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC structure
papers.approach: Alloy design with solid solution strengthening (without precipitates) to achieve a homogeneous microstructure that minimizes local galvanic variations; evaluation under acidic conditions and hydrogen environments
papers.findings: The alloy shows high tensile strength with over 90% elongation, excellent corrosion resistance in acidic media, and resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at room temperature.
papers.mechanism: A single-phase solid solution structure provides low hydrogen diffusivity and forms a stable, passivating oxide film that not only protects against corrosion but also reduces hydrogen uptake, thereby mitigating embrittlement.

established: Homogeneous and pure HEA coatings can be fabricated via processes like electrospark deposition to markedly enhance corrosion resistance.
Modifying grain boundary morphology (e.g., via inducing serration through controlled cooling) improves tensile ductility and creep rupture life by reducing strain localization.
Addition of elements such as Mo can concurrently enhance mechanical strength and corrosion resistance through microstructural refinement and improved passivation.

approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced surface hardness and excellent corrosion resistance in saline environments

approaches_tried.approach: Post heat treatment with reduced cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundaries
approaches_tried.outcome: Significant improvements in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life (increased by factors of 3.5 and 400, respectively) at high temperatures

approaches_tried.approach: Elemental modification through Mo addition during DED processing

mechanisms: Rapid cooling and inert atmosphere during deposition reduce oxidation and yield high-purity coatings that resist corrosion.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute local strains more evenly, delaying intergranular cracking and enhancing both ductility and creep resistance.
Mo addition promotes grain boundary segregation and σ-phase formation, which refines the microstructure and encourages the development of protective passivation films.
A homogeneous, single-phase solid solution minimizes local galvanic variations and reduces hydrogen diffusion, thereby enhancing both mechanical durability and resistance to hydrogen embrittlement.
disagreements: While post heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries has shown dramatic improvements in high-temperature creep and ductility, its effectiveness at room-temperature creep is less well documented.

Some studies indicate that Mo addition can increase hardness and corrosion resistance, yet there may be trade-offs with ductility—optimal concentration and processing conditions remain areas of debate.
open_questions: Can the beneficial effects of Mo addition simultaneously optimize room-temperature creep resistance, mechanical durability, and corrosion resistance in HEAs for aerospace fasteners?
How might the mechanisms observed at elevated temperatures (e.g., grain boundary serration) translate to room-temperature conditions relevant for fastener applications?

What are the optimal processing conditions (e.g., heat treatment profiles) when combining compositional modifications (like Mo addition) with microstructural engineering to achieve the desired balance?
opportunities: Investigate a single intervention that combines controlled Mo addition with optimized post-processing to induce beneficial microstructural features (such as serrated grain boundaries) in HEAs intended for aerospace fasteners.
Conduct long-term room-temperature creep and corrosion tests under aerospace-relevant environments to evaluate the durability improvements provided by Mo and related alloying strategies.

Explore additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., DED or laser cladding) that enable precise control of composition and microstructure to concurrently enhance mechanical durability, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.

directions.assessment: Directly addresses the combined need for enhanced mechanical durability, improved room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance. Prior studies indicate that 5–10% Mo addition refines the microstructure through grain‐boundary segregation and formation of σ phase particles, enhancing passivation film formation. The physics and evidence support this, though optimum level must be balanced against potential ductility loss.

Grain refinement by severe plastic deformation can improve yield strength and reduce creep strain through increased grain‐boundary area while also possibly refining surface passivation. This intervention is underpinned by well‐known mechanical principles though it may also risk embrittlement if overdone.

directions.direction: Surface engineering via electrospark deposition coating.
directions.assessment: Applying a high‐purity HEA coating (e.g. HfNbTaTiZr) by electrospark deposition improves corrosion resistance and surface hardness via rapid cooling in an inert atmosphere. It directly improves durability and corrosion resistance, though its effect on room‐temperature creep is more indirect.

directions.direction: Interstitial alloying (small C addition) in HEAs.
directions.assessment: Adding a controlled amount of an interstitial element (carbon) can enhance mechanical strength via solid–solution strengthening and promote beneficial mechanisms (e.g. nano‐twinning) that improve ductility and possibly corrosion resistance. However, the window between beneficial strengthening versus carbide formation is narrow.

directions.direction: Heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: Controlled slow cooling to promote serrated grain boundaries can reduce strain concentration and has been shown to significantly improve high‐temperature creep and ductility. However, its direct effect on room‐temperature creep is less established, which limits its direct applicability for aerospace fasteners operating at ambient conditions.

candidates.hypothesis: In a CrCoNiFe-based high-entropy alloy produced by directed energy deposition (DED), substituting ~5% of the alloying elements with Mo will concurrently improve mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
candidates.intervention: Addition of approximately 5 wt% Mo (replacing a portion of Cr or equivalent) during powder blending for DED processing.

candidates.hypothesis: Applying an electrospark-deposited high-purity HfNbTaTiZr HEA coating (with an optimized thickness of 20–30 μm and an engineered diffusion bond layer) on aerospace fasteners will improve overall durability by enhancing surface hardness, reducing localized room-temperature creep at contact points, and improving corrosion resistance and fatigue performance relative to uncoated fasteners.
candidates.intervention: Apply an optimized HfNbTaTiZr HEA coating using electrospark deposition under an argon atmosphere with rapid cooling, followed by an optional post-deposition heat treatment to relieve residual stresses and improve adhesion.
candidates.changes: Clarified that the electrospark-deposited HEA coating must be optimized in thickness (e.g., 20–30 μm) and adhesion through a diffusion bond interlayer and post-deposition heat treatment. Addressed concerns about coating defects, thermal expansion mismatch, and long‐term fatigue by explicitly incorporating additional mechanical and fatigue tests.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 wt% Mo during the powder blending stage of directed energy deposition (DED) for a CrCoNiFe-based high-entropy alloy will simultaneously improve mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 5 wt% Mo (with appropriate compositional adjustments) during powder blending prior to DED processing.
candidates.changes: Clarified that the Mo addition is specified as 5 wt% (with careful compositional control) and addressed potential trade-offs in ductility. Expanded the discussion on σ-phase formation and grain boundary segregation, with emphasis on process optimization to prevent embrittlement.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 0.5 at.% interstitial carbon during synthesis of a CrCoNiFe-based high-entropy alloy will enhance mechanical strength and ductility while reducing room-temperature creep rates and improving corrosion resistance compared to its undoped counterpart.
candidates.intervention: Introduce around 0.5 at.% carbon during alloy synthesis under controlled cooling conditions to ensure interstitial occupation without carbide precipitation.
candidates.changes: Specified that the interstitial addition is 0.5 at.% carbon and provided additional justification regarding the limited window to avoid carbide precipitation. Emphasized the need for controlling processing conditions (cooling rate, heat treatment) to maintain carbon in interstitial positions.

candidates.hypothesis: Reducing the grain size of a CrCoNiFe HEA by applying 75% cold rolling followed by appropriate post-deformation thermal treatment will improve mechanical durability, reduce room-temperature creep rates, and enhance corrosion resistance compared to the coarse-grained alloy.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to 75% cold rolling to achieve ultrafine grains (sub-micron to micron size) followed by a controlled annealing treatment to relieve residual stresses and maintain ductility.
candidates.changes: Extended the hypothesis to include post-cold rolling treatments to mitigate residual stresses and anisotropy. Addressed concerns regarding potential embrittlement and long-term stability by specifying the use of subsequent thermal annealing if necessary.
